archetypes.name: Half-wave slot in an infinite ground plane
archetypes.summary: Narrow rectangular slot of length ~lambda/2 cut in a large conducting screen, the Babinet complement of a half-wave strip dipole.
archetypes.notes: BABINET/BOOKER DERIVATION. Babinet's optical principle states that the fields of a screen and of its complement sum to the incident field. Booker (1946) extended it to vector electromagnetics: the complementary structure of a perfectly conducting screen is obtained by interchanging metal and aperture AND interchanging E and H. Write the slot problem as an equivalent magnetic-current sheet: the tangential E across the aperture, E_t = -n x M, drives a magnetic current M. The complementary electric-current dipole radiates with the same pattern shape but with E and H exchanged. Enforcing the duality transformation E -> H, H -> -E, eta0 -> 1/eta0 on the terminal quantities gives V_slot proportional to eta0*I_dipole/2 and I_slot proportional to 2*V_dipole/eta0, hence Z_slot = V_slot/I_slot = (eta0^2/4)*(I_dipole/V_dipole) = eta0^2/(4*Z_dipole). The factor of 4 (not 1) is the whole content of Booker's correction and comes from the two-sided radiation of a zero-thickness screen: the slot radiates into BOTH half spaces, so each side sees half the terminal current. Numerically eta0^2/4 = 376.730313412^2/4 = 35481.43 ohm^2. SIGN OF THE REACTANCE. With the classic thin half-wave dipole Z_d = 73.1 + j42.5 ohm (Balanis eq. 4-93, l = lambda/2 exactly, which is slightly LONGER than resonance, hence inductive), Z_s = 35481.43/(73.1 + j42.5) = 35481.43*(73.1 - j42.5)/(73.1^2 + 42.5^2) = 362.8 - j210.9 ohm. The slot is CAPACITIVE exactly where its complementary dipole is inductive, because Z_s is proportional to 1/Z_d and inversion conjugates the reactance sign. The magnitude 363 + j211 is very widely quoted (including in lecture notes and several handbooks) with a POSITIVE reactance; that printed sign is inconsistent with the +j42.5 dipole it is derived from. This spec returns the algebraically correct 362.8 - j210.9 ohm and exposes |Z| = 419.6 ohm and the 363/211 magnitudes separately so a user chasing the textbook numbers still finds them. The physical consequence is real: to tune a slot to resonance you SHORTEN it, exactly as for a dipole, because X_slot and X_dipole cross zero at the same electrical length (0.464 lambda at the default w/L = 0.05). RESTRICTION -- READ THIS BEFORE USING Z = 363 - j211. The relation Z_slot*Z_dipole = eta0^2/4 holds ONLY for (a) an INFINITE screen, (b) a PERFECTLY CONDUCTING screen, (c) a ZERO-THICKNESS screen, (d) free space on both sides, and (e) a complementary dipole that is the exact metal/aperture inverse of the slot (a STRIP dipole of width w, not a round wire; the equivalent round-wire radius is a = w/4). This is the single most misapplied result in the whole slot family. A slot in a finite ground plane, a slot with a cavity or a dielectric behind it, a slot in a thick wall, or a slot fed by a transmission line that loads one side, does NOT obey it. Closing off one half space (cavity backing, or a half-space mount) removes half the radiated power for the same aperture voltage, halving the radiation conductance and DOUBLING the impedance to ~726 - j422 ohm; that case is the cavity_backed_slot archetype. Finite screens ripple the impedance by +/-20% with screen size and add a rear lobe. PATTERN. Duality also fixes the pattern: the slot's far-field pattern SHAPE is identical to the complementary dipole's with E and H interchanged, so the directivity of the two-sided slot equals the dipole's, D0 = 1.643 (2.155 dBi). The plane containing the slot's long axis carries the 78 deg figure-of-eight cut (the dipole's E-plane, which for the slot is the H-plane); the plane perpendicular to the slot axis is uniform. Radiated E is PERPENDICULAR to the slot's long axis: a vertical slot radiates HORIZONTAL polarisation, the opposite of a vertical dipole, and this catches people out in practice. BANDWIDTH. Because Z_s = k/Z_d, the slot's Q equals the complementary strip dipole's, so the VSWR-2 fractional bandwidth about resonance is that of a strip dipole of width w. The returned bandwidth is a two-point engineering interpolation (8.5% at w/L = 0.02, 20.5% at w/L = 0.10) and is good to about +/-30%.

parameters.name: slot_length
parameters.description: Long dimension of the slot, end to end

parameters.name: width_to_length_ratio
parameters.description: Slot width / slot length. Auto-defaults to 0.05; raise it for more bandwidth, lower it for a narrower beam-free thin slot.

parameters.name: complementary_dipole_resistance
parameters.description: Input resistance of the complementary STRIP dipole at the same electrical length. Auto-defaults to 73.1 ohm, the classic l = lambda/2 thin-dipole value.

parameters.name: complementary_dipole_reactance
parameters.description: Input reactance of the complementary STRIP dipole at the same electrical length. Auto-defaults to +42.5 ohm (l = lambda/2 exactly, i.e. above resonance, inductive).

parameters.name: complementary_dipole_resonant_resistance
parameters.description: Resistance of the complementary dipole at ITS resonance (X = 0), where the slot is also resonant. DERIVED from the slot width through resonant_dipole's fit (75.8 ohm at the default w/L = 0.05); supply it to override.

parameters.name: complementary thickness parameter
parameters.description: log10(lambda0/a) of the complementary dipole, a = w/4

synthesis.notes: log10(lambda0/a) of the complementary dipole, a = w/4. The width is taken on a nominal 0.47*lambda0 length rather than on L itself, which would make the definition circular; solving it self-consistently moves L by 0.03% and Rd_res by 0.06%.

Driving-point resistance of the complementary dipole at its own resonance, from resonant_dipole's solved fit at the same thickness: 73.7 ohm at w/L = 0.02, 75.8 at 0.05. It replaces a flat 67 ohm, which was lower than a dipole of ANY thickness presents at resonance. The two independent solvers put it 0.6-2.5% lower than the fit (72.2-72.6 ohm at w/L = 0.02, 74.0-75.4 at 0.05; delta-gap resistance creeps with the mesh), so the slot resistances derived from it are good to about 3%. Supply Rd_res to override.

Resonant slot length. By Babinet a slot resonates where its complementary dipole does, and that dipole is a wire of radius a = w/4. This spec used to carry a flat 0.4785*lambda0, attributed to King's data, which is the resonant length of a much THINNER dipole. The length now comes from resonant_dipole's own length law at the complementary radius: 0.4855 lambda0 at w/L = 0.001, 0.4755 lambda0 at w/L = 0.01, 0.4709 lambda0 at w/L = 0.02, 0.4637 lambda0 at w/L = 0.05. Checked with two independent solvers, exact-kernel method of moments and Hallen's equation, on meshes each can be trusted at: 0.4704-0.4711 at w/L = 0.02 and 0.4645-0.4654 at 0.05. The law is inside 0.1% at the narrower width and 0.2-0.4% short at the default. Wider slots resonate shorter, exactly as fatter dipoles do.
Slot gap from the width ratio. w barely affects the pattern; it sets bandwidth and the resonant-length correction.
The exact lambda/2 reference length at which the quoted 362.8 - j210.9 ohm applies. The slot is NOT resonant here; it is capacitive.
Physical aperture area L*w. Of no use for directivity (the slot is not an aperture-limited radiator) but needed for mechanical work.

analysis.notes: Z_slot * Z_dipole = eta0^2/4 = 35481.43 ohm^2. Booker's relation. The constant is exact given eta0 = 376.730313412 ohm; the older eta = 120*pi convention gives 35530.6, a 0.14% difference.
Re{eta0^2/(4*Zd)}. With the default 73.1 + j42.5 dipole this is 362.8 ohm.
Im{eta0^2/(4*Zd)} = -eta0^2*Xd/(4*|Zd|^2). NEGATIVE for the default inductive dipole: -210.9 ohm. See the sign discussion in notes.
Complex form, 362.8 - j210.9 ohm by default. Two-sided infinite zero-thickness screen only.
|Zs| = (eta0^2/4)/|Zd| = 419.6 ohm for the default dipole.

Purely real slot impedance where X = 0, eta0^2/(4*Rd_res): 467.9 ohm at the default w/L = 0.05 and 481.7 at 0.02. The old flat Rd_res = 67 ohm gave 529.6, about 13% high. The shorthand 'a resonant slot is about 500 ohm' survives; the direction of the error does not - a wider slot has a fatter complement with MORE resistance, so it sits LOWER, not higher.

Same slot with one half space closed off (cavity backing or a half-space mount): the radiation conductance halves so the resistance doubles, 936 ohm at the default width. This is why cavity-backed slots are nearly always fed off-centre or through a transformer.
G = Re{Y_slot} = 4*Rd/eta0^2 = 2.060e-3 S for Rd = 73.1 ohm. The slot is naturally described by an admittance because it is a shunt element across whatever feeds it.
D0 = 1.6409 (2.1517 dBi), identical to the complementary half-wave dipole because Babinet preserves the pattern shape. Radiation is split between the two half spaces.
5.16 dBi if one half space is closed off (cavity-backed or flush half-space mount): the same power into half the solid angle.
Half-power beamwidth in the plane CONTAINING the slot's long axis -- the slot's H-plane, and the dual of the dipole's 78 deg E-plane cut.

In the plane PERPENDICULAR to the slot axis (the slot's E-plane) the pattern of an infinite zero-thickness screen is UNIFORM -- there are no half-power points, so 360 deg is returned as a sentinel meaning omnidirectional in that cut. A finite screen introduces edge-diffraction ripple of a few dB and a null in the screen plane.

Angle between the radiated E vector and the slot's LONG axis. Exactly 90 deg: a vertical slot radiates horizontal polarisation. Linear polarisation; cross-pol is set only by screen finiteness and feed asymmetry.

VSWR-2 bandwidth referenced to the resonant resistance. Engineering interpolation anchored at 8.5% for w/L = 0.02 and 20.5% for w/L = 0.10, derived from the complementary strip dipole's measured bandwidth (the slot's Q equals the dipole's because Zs = k/Zd). Good to about +/-30%. Do not extrapolate beyond w/L = 0.2.
Q from the VSWR-2 bandwidth using the Yaghjian-Best relation FBW = (s-1)/(Q*sqrt(s)) with s = 2, i.e. Q = 0.7071/FBW. Inherits the bandwidth model's +/-30%.

validity: INFINITE, perfectly conducting, ZERO-THICKNESS screen. This is the restriction on Booker's relation and it is routinely ignored. A screen smaller than about 2*lambda on a side changes the impedance by tens of percent and adds a rear lobe
free space on BOTH sides of the screen. Any cavity, dielectric or transmission line on one side breaks the two-sided symmetry the factor of 4 encodes
narrow slot, w << lambda (w/L < 0.2). Wider slots depart from the complementary strip-dipole model and start to behave as apertures
the complementary radiator is a STRIP dipole of width w, equivalent to a round wire of radius a = w/4 -- not a round wire of radius w/2
quoted Z assumes the feed is at the slot CENTRE. Feeding off-centre multiplies the impedance by cos^2(pi*x/L) (see cavity_backed_slot)
wall thickness t must satisfy t << w, otherwise the slot behaves as a short length of below-cutoff waveguide and its resonant length grows
the 78 deg / omnidirectional beamwidths apply to a lambda/2 slot; longer slots break up into multiple lobes exactly as a long dipole does

the resonant length and resistance come from the complementary dipole's laws, confirmed against two independent solvers up to w/L = 0.05 (a = 0.0058 lambda0). Wider slots are extrapolation: their complementary wire is too fat for a delta-gap feed to be solved honestly here, and the reduced-kernel Hallen solution already drifts at 0.05 under a fine mesh

known_cases.source: Complementary dipole of radius a = w/4 = 0.00580 lambda0 at the default w/L = 0.05, with the slot length solved self-consistently: resonant_dipole's length law gives 0.46379 lambda0 and its solved resistance 75.80 ohm, so the resonant slot is 468.1 ohm. Exact-kernel MoM and Hallen's equation independently give 0.4645-0.4654 lambda0 and 74.0-75.4 ohm, a 471-479 ohm slot. lambda0 = 0.99930819 m at 300 MHz.

Narrower slot, thinner complement (a = 0.00235 lambda0): resonant_dipole gives 0.47087 lambda0 and 73.67 ohm, so the slot is LONGER and HIGHER in resistance, 481.6 ohm. Exact-kernel MoM and Hallen give 0.4704-0.4711 lambda0 and 72.2-72.6 ohm.
Booker 1946; Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., eq. 12-11 (Zs*Zd = eta^2/4); eta0 = 376.730313412 ohm
Babinet/Booker applied to the classic lambda/2 dipole 73.1 + j42.5 ohm. Magnitudes 363 and 211 are the textbook values; the reactance sign is negative -- see notes
Rd_res supplied, so the derived value is overridden: 67 ohm, the flat figure this spec used to assume, reproduces its old 529.6 ohm and the one-sided doubling used in every cavity-backed slot design
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., eq. 4-91 (D0 = 1.643 for a lambda/2 dipole) carried through Babinet; HPBW 78 deg from eq. 4-65
Strip-dipole bandwidth interpolation (8.5% at w/L = 0.02, 20.5% at w/L = 0.10); Q from Yaghjian & Best FBW = (s-1)/(Q*sqrt(s))

references: H. G. Booker, 'Slot aerials and their relation to complementary wire aerials (Babinet's principle)', J. IEE 93 Part IIIA, pp. 620-626, 1946
Balanis, Antenna Theory: Analysis and Design, 4th ed., Ch. 12.1-12.2 (Babinet's principle, slot impedance)
Balanis, Antenna Theory, 4th ed., eqs. 4-91, 4-93 (half-wave dipole D0 = 1.643, Zin = 73 + j42.5)
Kraus & Marhefka, Antennas for All Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 9 (slot antennas, complementary impedance)
Volakis (ed.), Antenna Engineering Handbook, 4th ed., Ch. 13 (slot antennas)
Yaghjian & Best, 'Impedance, Bandwidth and Q of Antennas', IEEE T-AP 53(4), 2005

archetypes.name: Cavity-backed rectangular slot
archetypes.summary: Half-wave slot over a shorted cavity, making the pattern unidirectional.

synthesis.notes: slightly under lambda/2, as with a dipole
width sets the bandwidth; 5% of the length is a typical starting point

A quarter-wave deep cavity transforms the short at the back wall into an open circuit at the slot, so it does not load the slot. This depth is the whole reason the cavity works, and it is inherently narrowband.

analysis.notes: Radiating into a half space instead of a full one doubles the impedance of the equivalent open slot, so roughly 726 ohm at resonance.
unidirectional, so twice the open slot's directivity: about 5.16 dBi
Indicative: the quarter-wave cavity is resonant, so the cavity-backed slot trades roughly half the open slot's bandwidth for its unidirectional pattern.

validity: cavity depth is correct at one frequency only; the structure is narrowband by construction
assumes a cavity at least a half wave across laterally, or the cavity modes shift the resonance
bandwidth entry is indicative, not derived

known_cases.source: 1 GHz: 0.48 lambda slot = 143.9 mm over a lambda/4 = 74.95 mm cavity; unidirectional directivity is 2x the open slot. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 12

references: Elliott, Antenna Theory and Design, revised ed., Ch. 8

archetypes.name: Waveguide longitudinal shunt slot
archetypes.summary: Broad-wall slot offset from the centreline; the element of every slotted-waveguide array.

synthesis.notes: resonant slot length, trimmed from lambda/2 by the finite slot width

analysis.notes: Stevenson's peak normalised conductance: g1 = 2.09*(lambda_g/lambda)*(a/b)*cos^2(pi*lambda/(2*lambda_g)) - note this is the value at maximum offset, and the leading lambda ratio is inverted relative to some printings, so cross-check against the source before building an array.
g = g1*sin^2(pi*x1/a). The sin^2 offset law is exact in Stevenson's theory and is what lets an array designer set each element's coupling by displacement alone.
A resonant standing-wave array needs the shunt conductances to sum to 1 for a matched input; this is how many identical slots at this offset that would take.

validity: a slot on the centreline (x1 = 0) does not cut longitudinal current and therefore does not radiate at all - the sin^2 law makes this explicit
Stevenson's theory assumes a thin wall and a narrow slot
single-mode TE10 operation
mutual coupling between adjacent slots is NOT modelled and matters in real arrays
the g1 expression should be cross-checked against the source before committing an array design to fabrication

known_cases.source: A centreline slot cuts no transverse current and radiates nothing: sin^2(0) = 0. This is the defining property of the longitudinal shunt slot. Stevenson, Theory of Slots in Rectangular Waveguides, J. Appl. Phys. 19, 1948
An offset of a/2 is the maximum-coupling position, where sin^2(pi/2) = 1. Stevenson, Theory of Slots in Rectangular Waveguides, J. Appl. Phys. 19, 1948
WR-90 at 10 GHz: TE10 cutoff 6.556 GHz, guide wavelength 39.73 mm. Pozar, Microwave Engineering 4th ed., Ch. 3

references: Stevenson, Theory of Slots in Rectangular Waveguides, J. Appl. Phys. 19, 1948
Elliott, Antenna Theory and Design, revised ed., Ch. 8

archetypes.name: Resonant longitudinal slot array
archetypes.summary: Standing-wave waveguide array: slots every half guide wavelength, offsets alternating, all in phase at broadside.

synthesis.notes: resonant length, slightly short of a half wavelength
Half a GUIDE wavelength, which is longer than half a free-space wavelength. The 180 degrees of propagation phase between neighbours is undone by putting them on opposite sides of the centreline.
Each slot takes 1/N of the guide conductance, from g = g1*sin^2(pi*x/a). Larger offsets couple harder, so a short array needs slots further out.

analysis.notes: conductance of a slot at the guide wall, before the sin^2 offset factor
By design: N slots in shunt, each 1/N, sum to a matched unity conductance
Always above 0.5 and below 1 for a propagating TE10 guide, so the array is safe from grating lobes but its sidelobes sit higher than a half-wave-spaced array's
Uniform broadside array factor, D = 2*N*d/lambda0. The element pattern and the guide's own width add roughly 2-3 dB on top; this figure is the array factor alone.
uniform excitation. Tapering the offsets lowers this, at the cost of aperture efficiency - see the arrays module for Chebyshev and Taylor weights.

INDICATIVE. A resonant array is a standing-wave structure: all slots go out of phase together as frequency moves, and the usable band narrows roughly as 1/N. This is the price paid for broadside operation.

validity: N*g1 must exceed 1, or the required offset has no solution - a long array needs slots too weakly coupled to reach unity total
resonant (standing-wave) operation: the guide is short-circuited a quarter guide wavelength beyond the last slot, and the whole array is narrowband
mutual coupling between slots is neglected, and it is not negligible in practice - real designs iterate offsets full-wave
uniform excitation assumed; the offsets here are all equal

known_cases.source: WR-90 at 10 GHz: guide wavelength 39.71 mm, so slots sit 19.85 mm apart - a third more than the 15.0 mm free-space half wavelength. Twelve slots each take 1/12 of the conductance.
g1 = 2.09*(lambda0/lambda_g)*(a/b)*cos^2(pi*lambda0/2*lambda_g) = 0.499 for WR-90 at 10 GHz. Solving sin^2(pi*x/a) = 1/(12*g1) puts the slots 3.06 mm off the centreline, 13.4% of the broad wall.
Eleven gaps of 19.85 mm span 218.4 mm; the uniform array factor gives 2*12*0.6622 = 15.89 = 12.02 dBi

references: Elliott, Antenna Theory and Design, revised ed., Ch. 8 (slot arrays)
Stevenson, Theory of slots in rectangular waveguides, J. Appl. Phys. 19, 1948

archetypes.name: Travelling-wave longitudinal slot array
archetypes.summary: Slots spaced off half a guide wavelength so the beam squints, ending in a matched load instead of a short.

parameters.name: spacing in guide wavelengths
parameters.description: 0.5 gives broadside; away from 0.5 the beam squints

analysis.notes: sin(theta) = beta/k0 - lambda0/(2d). The second term is the 180 degrees the alternating offsets add per element. At d = lambda_g/2 the two cancel exactly and the beam is broadside.
Positive is toward the load. Spacings BELOW lambda_g/2 squint the beam back toward the feed.
uniform aperture, widened by 1/cos(theta) because a scanned aperture presents a shorter projection
Whatever is not radiated by the last slot is burnt in the load. Five percent, a common target, costs 0.22 dB.
line-source directivity 2L/lambda, foreshortened by cos(theta) and reduced by the load loss
the spacing that would give broadside - deliberately avoided here, because at broadside every slot reflects in phase and the input match collapses

validity: d must stay clear of lambda_g/2: at exactly broadside the slot reflections add in phase and the array will not match. That is the reason this variant exists
d/lambda0 below 1 to keep grating lobes out of real space
uniform slot excitation assumed; a real travelling-wave array tapers the offsets along the guide to hold the aperture distribution as power drains away
beam angle shifts with frequency - useful for frequency scanning, a nuisance otherwise

known_cases.source: The defining check: at d = lambda_g/2 the propagation phase and the alternating-offset phase cancel exactly, giving a broadside beam. Expectation of zero, so an absolute tolerance.
WR-90 at 10 GHz: beta/k0 = 0.75509, d = 23.82 mm, so sin(theta) = 0.75509 - 0.62926 = 0.12583 and the beam sits 7.23 deg off broadside
Below half a guide wavelength the beam squints the other way, back toward the feed - sin(theta) = 0.75509 - 0.83899 = -0.08390

references: Elliott, Antenna Theory and Design, revised ed., Ch. 8
Oliner & Jackson, Leaky-wave antennas, in Antenna Engineering Handbook 4th ed.

archetypes.name: Folded slot
archetypes.summary: Babinet dual of the folded dipole: folding steps the slot impedance DOWN by N squared, into coplanar-waveguide territory.

parameters.name: dual dipole resonant resistance
parameters.description: Resistance of the complementary dipole at ITS resonance (X = 0), where the slot is also resonant. DERIVED from the slot width through resonant_dipole's fit (75.8 ohm at the default w/L = 0.05); supply it to override.

parameters.name: complementary thickness parameter
parameters.description: log10(lambda0/a) of the complementary dipole, a = w/4

synthesis.notes: log10(lambda0/a) of the complementary dipole, a = w/4. The width is taken on a nominal 0.47*lambda0 length rather than on L itself, which would make the definition circular; solving it self-consistently moves L by 0.03% and Rd_res by 0.06%.

Driving-point resistance of the complementary dipole at its own resonance, from resonant_dipole's solved fit at the same thickness: 73.7 ohm at w/L = 0.02, 75.8 at 0.05. It replaces a flat 67 ohm, which was lower than a dipole of ANY thickness presents at resonance. The two independent solvers put it 0.6-2.5% lower than the fit (72.2-72.6 ohm at w/L = 0.02, 74.0-75.4 at 0.05; delta-gap resistance creeps with the mesh), so the slot resistances derived from it are good to about 3%. Supply Rd_res to override.

Same resonant length as a plain slot of the same width - folding changes the impedance, not the resonance. By Babinet a slot resonates where its complementary dipole does, and that dipole is a wire of radius a = w/4. This spec used to carry a flat 0.4785*lambda0, attributed to King's data, which is the resonant length of a much THINNER dipole. The length now comes from resonant_dipole's own length law at the complementary radius: 0.4855 lambda0 at w/L = 0.001, 0.4755 lambda0 at w/L = 0.01, 0.4709 lambda0 at w/L = 0.02, 0.4637 lambda0 at w/L = 0.05. Checked with two independent solvers, exact-kernel method of moments and Hallen's equation, on meshes each can be trusted at: 0.4704-0.4711 at w/L = 0.02 and 0.4645-0.4654 at 0.05. The law is inside 0.1% at the narrower width and 0.2-0.4% short at the default.

analysis.notes: Babinet: Z_slot * Z_dipole = eta0^2/4. A resonant slot in an infinite screen sits near 468 ohm at the default width - far too high to feed directly.
The DUAL of the folded dipole's N^2 step-up. Where folding a dipole raises impedance, folding a slot lowers it - which is the whole point, because slots start too high.
117 ohm for the usual two-slot case, against 468 for a single slot. This is why folded slots and coplanar waveguide go together.
Doubled, for a slot backed by a cavity or a reflector so it radiates into a half space only
the folded slot radiates as a single slot does - the folding is a feed transformation, not an aperture change
cavity-backed
same width-driven estimate as the plain slot; folding does not much change the bandwidth
a slot's electric field lies ACROSS its long axis, at right angles to the equivalent dipole's

validity: infinite, perfectly conducting, zero-thickness screen - the Babinet condition. A real folded slot on a finite substrate reads lower and complex
the N^2 law assumes equal slot widths and close spacing, exactly as the folded dipole's does
Rd_res is derived from the slot width through the complementary dipole and can be supplied to override; it moves every impedance here
substrate loading shortens the resonant length, which this free-space form does not model

the resonant length and resistance come from the complementary dipole's laws, confirmed against two independent solvers up to w/L = 0.05 (a = 0.0058 lambda0). Wider slots are extrapolation: their complementary wire is too fat for a delta-gap feed to be solved honestly here, and the reduced-kernel Hallen solution already drifts at 0.05 under a fine mesh

known_cases.source: N = 1 must reduce to the plain slot: eta0^2/(4*75.80) = 468.1 ohm at the default w/L = 0.05, matching this family's half_wave_slot exactly
Two slots quarter the impedance: 468.1/4 = 117.0 ohm. The dual of the folded dipole, which QUADRUPLES its resistance - the same factor, the other way up.
Three slots give 468.1/9 = 52.0 ohm, close to a direct 50 ohm feed
Rd_res supplied overrides the derived value: the old flat 67 ohm gives 529.6/4 = 132.4 ohm, as this spec used to quote

references: Booker, Slot aerials and their relation to complementary wire aerials, JIEE 93, 1946
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 12.6 (Babinet's principle)
Tsai & York, FDTD analysis of CPW-fed folded-slot antennas, IEEE T-AP 44(2), 1996
